newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Germany fears guns, drugs influx across borders.
newsitem.headline: Germany fears guns, drugs influx across borders.

text.p: Germany is worried about an influx of guns, drugs and illegal immigrants via Austria, Italy and Greece but a Bonn official denied on Tuesday that this would disqualify these states for full membership in the open-border Schengen pact.

"We have special concerns about the controls at some borders outside the Schengen area," Kurt Schelter, State Secretary in the German Interior Ministry, said on on the sidelines of a Schengen executive committee meeting.

The meeting, in Lisbon, discussed plans for full membership of Austria, Greece and Italy in the Schengen agreement, which provides for border controls between European Union member states to be removed and for increased cooperation in police matters.
Greece's parliament adopted Schengen this month.
Schelter, spokesman for the German delegation at the meeting, denied a report in the German newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung that Germany would block entry to Schengen for Austria, Greece and Italy.
"There is no veto. It is just our concern to be wise in promoting this free movement (of people) in Europe.
"Germany never issued a veto. We feel it will be possible to bring down border controls (in Austria, Greece and Italy) step by step," he said.
"It is not an easy border between Italy and Albania -- in the Mediterranean Sea -- and even the Hungarian border, between Austria and Hungary, is a very risky one."
He told Reuters: "We want to be sure that our friends in Italy and Austria make all efforts they can to improve controls at the external Schengen borders."
Asked if Germany was concerned about a possible influx of guns from chaotic Albania following an insurrection there earlier this year, Schelter said:
"Certainly. And illegal immigrants (from Albania) across the borders to Austria."
He said Germany was concerned about smuggling of illicit drugs into the country via Hungary and Austria.
"We have to prevent drug trafficking coming across the Hungarian border to Austria (and then Germany).
"In Poland, there are some factories and laboratories at which synthetic drugs are produced. That is a big threat coming from Poland to Germany," he added.
The executive committee meeting was held in Lisbon because Portugal holds the six-month rotating presidency of Schengen until the end of June.

France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Spain, Portugal and Germany are all full Schengen members. Greece, Austria, Italy, Denmark, Finland and Sweden have signed but not yet fully implemented the pact.
